The House of Garen was the ruling hereditary dynasty of the Ajuran Empire.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Crescent-19) Its origin lies in the Garen Kingdom that during the 13th century ruled parts of the Somali Region of Ethiopia.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-20) With the migration of Somalis from the northern half of the Horn region southwards, new cultural and religious orders were introduced, influencing the administrative structure of the dynasty.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-21)
A system of governance began to evolve into an Islamic government. Through their genealogical Baraka, which came from the saint _Balad_ (who was known to have come from outside the Kingdom).[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-24)

### Rise to prominence and dominance
[edit]
The Ajuran gradually became a notable and respected empire.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTENjoku201340-3) They rose to dominance in the interior of the Banaadir region in the late 1300s, after which they maintained hegemony for approximately three centuries. The introduction of a great variety of technological innovations are attributed to the empire, such as systems of dykes and dams on the Shebelle River, large homes and stone fortifications along with the creation of large stone wells, many of which were still in use well into the 20th century. Notably, the Ajuran were the first to impose a regular system of tribute on the surrounding populations.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-:3-25) The empire fielded a powerful army which employed firearms towards the end of its dominant period. As a 'water dynasty', the Ajuran monopolized the Jubba and Shabelle rivers through hydraulic engineering.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-:2-8)

### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
Over the next decades tensions remained high and the increased contact between Somali sailors and Ottomancorsairs worried the Portuguese who sent a punitive expedition under João de Sepúlveda, where he bombarded Mogadishu and captured Turkish vessels, compelling its ruler to sign a peace deal with the Portuguese. Barawa would also sign peace with the Portuguese after being sacked.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-52)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Sep%C3%BAlveda,_1542-53) The Ottoman-Somali cooperation against the Portuguese on the Indian Ocean reached a high point in the 1580s when Ajuran clients of the coastal cities began to cooperate with the Arabs and Swahilis under Portuguese rule and sent an envoy to the Turkish corsair Mir Ali Bey for a joint expedition against the Portuguese. He agreed and was joined by a Somali fleet in order to attack the Portuguese colonies in Southeast Africa.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch195025-54)
A 16th century map by Jan Huyghen[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-55)

### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
The Somali-Ottoman offensive managed to drive out the Portuguese from several important cities such as Pate, Mombasa and Kilwa. However, the Portuguese governor sent envoys to Portuguese India requesting a large Portuguese fleet. This request was answered and it reversed the previous offensive of the Muslims into one of defense. The Portuguese armada managed to re-take most of the lost cities and began punishing their leaders, but they refrained from attacking Mogadishu, securing the city's autonomy in the Indian Ocean.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Cites-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-57) The Ottoman Empire would remain an economic partner.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Shapes-12) Throughout the 16th and 17th centuries the Ajurans successively defied Portuguese hegemony on the Indian Ocean by employing a new coinage which followed the Ottoman pattern, thus proclaiming an attitude of economic independence in regard to the Portuguese.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-61)

### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
From the late 15th and up until the 17th centuries saw the arrival of Muslim families from Arabia, Persia, India and Spain to the Ajuran realm of territories, the majority of whom settled in the coastal provinces. Some migrated because of the instability in their respective regions, as was the case with the Hadhrami families from Yemen and Muslims from Spain fleeing the Inquisition.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-62)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-63) Others came to conduct business or for religious purposes. Due to their strong tradition in religious learning, the new Muslim communities also enjoyed high status among the Somali ruling elite and commoners.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-65)
The tomb of Sheikh Hussein
The most famous Somali scholar of Islam from the Ajuraan period is Sheikh Hussein, who was born in Merca, one of the power jurisdiction and cultural centers of the Ajuran Empire.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-66) He is credited with converting the Sidamo people living in the area of what is now the Bale Province, Ethiopia to Islam.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-67) He is also credited with establishing the Sultanate of Bale.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-69)
Despite the Bale Sultanate not being directly under Ajuran rule, the two kingdoms were deeply connected and Bale was heavily influenced by Ajuran. His tomb lies in the town of Sheikh Hussein in what is considered the most sacred place in the country for Ethiopian Muslims, in particular those of Oromo ethnic descent.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-71)

### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
In the mid-17th century, the Oromo people collectively began expanding from their homeland towards the southern Somali coast at a time when the Ajurans were at the height of their power.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECassanelli1982114-72) The Garen rulers conducted several military expeditions known as the _Gaal Madow_ _Wars,_ on the Oromo invaders, converting those that were captured to Islam.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-73)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-74)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-75)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-76)

### Fall of Benadir and Southern Somalia
[edit]
The Ajuran Empire slowly declined in power at the end of the 17th century. In this period the rulers of the empire abandoned Sharia, became oppressive and enacted heavy taxation.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-:4-9) The dethronement of the Muzaffar clients in Mogadishu and other coastal cities by the Abgaalimam who then established the Hiraab Imamate taking residence in Mogadishu was a significant setback,[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTELewis198837-77) and the defeat of the Silcis vassals by a former Ajuran general in the interior of the state, Ibrahim Adeer, who established the Gobroon dynasty.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-78)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Lewis_1960_213%E2%80%93230-79) By the early 1700s there was effectively no trace of Ajuran left in Banaadir.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-:3-25)
Taxation and the practice of primae noctis were the main catalysts for the revolts against Ajuran rulers.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-80) The loss of port cities and fertile farms meant that much needed sources of revenue were lost to the rebels.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Lewis_1960_213%E2%80%93230-79) Somali maritime enterprise significantly declined after the collapse of the Ajuran Empire. However, other principalities such as the Isaaq Sultanate, Warsangali Sultanate, Majeerteen Sultanate, and the Sultanate of Hobyo in a way ensured its continuity.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-81)

### Fall of Benadir and Southern Somalia
The city of Merca was a prominent administrative center of the Ajurans
The Ajuran nobility used many of the typical Somali aristocratic and court titles, with the Garen rulers styled Imam.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-82) These leaders were the empire's highest authority, and counted multiple Sultans, Emirs, and Kings as clients or vassals. The Garen rulers also had seasonal palaces in Mareeg, Qelafo and Merca, important cities in the Empire were Mogadishu and Barawa. The state religion was Islam, and thus law was based on Sharia.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-83)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-84)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-85)
1.   Imam – Head of State[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-86)  
2.   Emir – Commander of the armed forces and navy  
3.   [Na'ibs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Na'ib "Na'ib") – Viceroys[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-87)  
4.   Wazirs – Tax and revenue collectors  
5.   Qadis – Chief Judges

### Fall of Benadir and Southern Somalia
Through their control of the region's wells, the Garen rulers effectively held a monopoly over their nomadic subjects as they were the only hydraulic empire in Africa during their reign. Large wells made out of limestone were constructed throughout the state, which attracted Somali and Oromo nomads with their livestock.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Siedlak-88) The centralized regulations of the wells made it easier for the nomads to settle disputes by taking their queries to government officials who would act as mediators. Long distance caravan trade, a long-time practice in the Horn of Africa, continued unchanged in Ajuran times. Today, numerous ruined and abandoned towns throughout the interior of Somalia and the Horn of Africa are evidence of a once-booming inland trade network dating from the medieval period.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECassanelli1982149-89)
The Jubba River
With the centralized supervision of the Ajuran, farms in Afgooye, Kismayo and other areas in the Jubba and Shabelle valleys increased their productivity. A system of irrigation ditches known locally as _Kelliyo_ fed directly from the Shebelle and Jubba rivers into the plantations where sorghum, maize, beans, grain and cotton were grown during the _gu_ (Spring in Somali) and _xagaa_ (Summer in Somali) seasons of the Somali calendar. This irrigation system was supported by numerous dikes and dams. To determine the average size of a farm, a land measurement system was also invented with _moos_, _taraab_ and _guldeed_ being the terms used.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-90)
Mogadishan currency
The State collected tribute from the farmers in the form of harvested products like durra, sorghum and bun, and from the nomads, cattle, camels and goats. The collecting of tribute was done by a wazir. Luxury goods imported from foreign lands were also presented as gifts to the Garen rulers by the coastal sultans of the state.

### Fall of Benadir and Southern Somalia
A political device that was implemented by the Garen rulers in their realm was a form of _ius primae noctis_,[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-91) which enabled them to create marriages that enforced their hegemonic rule over all the important groups of the empire. The rulers would also claim a large portion of the bride's wealth, which at the time was 100 camels.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Siedlak-88)
For trade, the Ajuran Empire minted its own Ajuran currency.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Stgi-92) It also utilized the Mogadishan currency originally minted by the Sultanate of Mogadishu, which later became incorporated into the Ajuran Empire.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Cites-56) Mogadishan coins have been found as far away as present-day United Arab Emirates in the Middle East.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Ncaaroth-93)

,  A.  Location  Thailand  is  in  the  center  of  Southeast  Asia,  or,  as   
it  is  also  called,  the  Indochinese  Peninsula  because  this  region   
is  a  peninsula  between  India  and  China.  Thailand  lies  between   
5°  37'  and  20°  27'  north  latitude  and  between  97°  22'  and  105°
37 *  east  longitude.
It  is  1,620  kilometers  long  at  its  longest  points  (north  -   
from  Maesai  District  of  Chiangrai  Province;  south  -  to  Betong   
District  of  Yala  Province).
It  is  750  kilometers  wide  at  its  widest  points  (west  -  from   
the  border  pass  of  Prachedi  Samong,  Thongphaphumi  District,  Kan-   
chanaburi  Province;  east  -  to  Chongmet,  Phibunmangsaban  District,   
Ubonratchathani  Province) . ,
It  is  10.1  kilometers  wide  at  its  narrowest  points  ;(west  -   
from  11°  42.4'  north  latitude;  east  -  to  Pakhuaiwathoon ,  Khlong-   
wan  Township,  Huang  District,  Prachuabkhirikhan  Province.)
B.  Bound? ri-es  To  the  north  Thailand  borders  Burma  and  Laos;  to  the   
east  it  borders  Laos  and  Cambodia;  to  the  south  it  borders  the   
Gulf  of  Siam  and  Malaysia;  to  the  west  it  borders  Burma,  the  Sea   
of  Andaman  and  the  Strait  of  Malacca.

meters,  of  which  2,420  kilometers  are  seacoast  (1,930  kilometers   
along  the  Gulf  of  Siam  and  490  kilometers  along  the  Sea  of  Andaman   
and  the  Strait  of  Malacca).  This  leaves  3>400  kilometers  of  land   
border.
C.  Geography  Includes:  1.  lowlying  plains  area  which  floods  during

waters,  and  many  inter-connected  waterways;  2.  mountainous

to  the  various  plains  and  rivers  forming  valleys,  some  wide  and   
some  narrow  depending  on  the  terrain;  3.  high  plateaus  which,   
for  the  most  part,  are  sparsely  wooded  and  rolling.

the  northern,  central,  northeastern  and  southern.

The  nationalities  of  Thailand,  differentiated  according  to  language   
and  customs,  are  listed  as  follows.
1)  Thai.  Apart  from  the  chief  Thai  people,  there  are  also:
a)  Thai  Yai,  Kheun,  and  Leu.  These  tribes  originate  in  the  Thai   
Yai  territory  in  Burma  and  in  the  Sip  song  Panna  region  of  China.  In  Thai¬   
land  they  are  found  chiefly  in  the  northern  districts  of  Maehongson,   
Chiangmai,  and  Chiangrai  and  Lampong.  (For  the  Kheun,  see  the  Royal  Acad¬   
emy’s  Encyclopedia.)
b)  Phu  Thai,  Phuan,  and  Seung.  These  tribes’  place  of  origin  is   
in  the  Sam  Neua  and  Xieng  Khouang  (5th  and  6th  districts)  areas  in  Laos.
In  Thailand  the  Phu  Thais  are  found  in  Sakon  Nakhon  and  Nakhon  Phanom  in   
the  Northeast  Region.  The  Phuan  and  Seung  live  in  scattered  groups  in  the   
Central  Region,  especially  in  the  Sukhothai,  Lopburi,  Saraburi,  Rachaburi   
and  Kanchonburi  areas.  The  languages  of  these  three  tribes  are  very  simi¬   
lar  and  they  must  be  classified  as  belonging  to  the  same  branch  as  the   
Thai.

The  nationalities  of  Thailand,  differentiated  according  to  language   
and  customs,  are  listed  as  follows.
1)  Thai.  Apart  from  the  chief  Thai  people,  there  are  also:
a)  Thai  Yai,  Kheun,  and  Leu.  These  tribes  originate  in  the  Thai   
Yai  territory  in  Burma  and  in  the  Sip  song  Panna  region  of  China.  In  Thai¬   
land  they  are  found  chiefly  in  the  northern  districts  of  Maehongson,   
Chiangmai,  and  Chiangrai  and  Lampong.  (For  the  Kheun,  see  the  Royal  Acad¬   
emy’s  Encyclopedia.)
b)  Phu  Thai,  Phuan,  and  Seung.  These  tribes’  place  of  origin  is   
in  the  Sam  Neua  and  Xieng  Khouang  (5th  and  6th  districts)  areas  in  Laos.
In  Thailand  the  Phu  Thais  are  found  in  Sakon  Nakhon  and  Nakhon  Phanom  in   
the  Northeast  Region.  The  Phuan  and  Seung  live  in  scattered  groups  in  the   
Central  Region,  especially  in  the  Sukhothai,  Lopburi,  Saraburi,  Rachaburi   
and  Kanchonburi  areas.  The  languages  of  these  three  tribes  are  very  simi¬   
lar  and  they  must  be  classified  as  belonging  to  the  same  branch  as  the   
Thai.

Title: Ajuran Sultanate
Chunks: 9,10,11,12,13
### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
Over the next decades tensions remained high and the increased contact between Somali sailors and Ottomancorsairs worried the Portuguese who sent a punitive expedition under João de Sepúlveda, where he bombarded Mogadishu and captured Turkish vessels, compelling its ruler to sign a peace deal with the Portuguese. Barawa would also sign peace with the Portuguese after being sacked.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-52)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Sep%C3%BAlveda,_1542-53) The Ottoman-Somali cooperation against the Portuguese on the Indian Ocean reached a high point in the 1580s when Ajuran clients of the coastal cities began to cooperate with the Arabs and Swahilis under Portuguese rule and sent an envoy to the Turkish corsair Mir Ali Bey for a joint expedition against the Portuguese. He agreed and was joined by a Somali fleet in order to attack the Portuguese colonies in Southeast Africa.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch195025-54)
A 16th century map by Jan Huyghen[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-55)

### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
The Somali-Ottoman offensive managed to drive out the Portuguese from several important cities such as Pate, Mombasa and Kilwa. However, the Portuguese governor sent envoys to Portuguese India requesting a large Portuguese fleet. This request was answered and it reversed the previous offensive of the Muslims into one of defense. The Portuguese armada managed to re-take most of the lost cities and began punishing their leaders, but they refrained from attacking Mogadishu, securing the city's autonomy in the Indian Ocean.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Cites-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-57) The Ottoman Empire would remain an economic partner.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Shapes-12) Throughout the 16th and 17th centuries the Ajurans successively defied Portuguese hegemony on the Indian Ocean by employing a new coinage which followed the Ottoman pattern, thus proclaiming an attitude of economic independence in regard to the Portuguese.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-61)

### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
From the late 15th and up until the 17th centuries saw the arrival of Muslim families from Arabia, Persia, India and Spain to the Ajuran realm of territories, the majority of whom settled in the coastal provinces. Some migrated because of the instability in their respective regions, as was the case with the Hadhrami families from Yemen and Muslims from Spain fleeing the Inquisition.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-62)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-63) Others came to conduct business or for religious purposes. Due to their strong tradition in religious learning, the new Muslim communities also enjoyed high status among the Somali ruling elite and commoners.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-65)
The tomb of Sheikh Hussein
The most famous Somali scholar of Islam from the Ajuraan period is Sheikh Hussein, who was born in Merca, one of the power jurisdiction and cultural centers of the Ajuran Empire.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-66) He is credited with converting the Sidamo people living in the area of what is now the Bale Province, Ethiopia to Islam.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-67) He is also credited with establishing the Sultanate of Bale.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-69)
Despite the Bale Sultanate not being directly under Ajuran rule, the two kingdoms were deeply connected and Bale was heavily influenced by Ajuran. His tomb lies in the town of Sheikh Hussein in what is considered the most sacred place in the country for Ethiopian Muslims, in particular those of Oromo ethnic descent.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-71)

### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
In the mid-17th century, the Oromo people collectively began expanding from their homeland towards the southern Somali coast at a time when the Ajurans were at the height of their power.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECassanelli1982114-72) The Garen rulers conducted several military expeditions known as the _Gaal Madow_ _Wars,_ on the Oromo invaders, converting those that were captured to Islam.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-73)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-74)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-75)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-76)

### Fall of Benadir and Southern Somalia
[edit]
The Ajuran Empire slowly declined in power at the end of the 17th century. In this period the rulers of the empire abandoned Sharia, became oppressive and enacted heavy taxation.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-:4-9) The dethronement of the Muzaffar clients in Mogadishu and other coastal cities by the Abgaalimam who then established the Hiraab Imamate taking residence in Mogadishu was a significant setback,[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTELewis198837-77) and the defeat of the Silcis vassals by a former Ajuran general in the interior of the state, Ibrahim Adeer, who established the Gobroon dynasty.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-78)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Lewis_1960_213%E2%80%93230-79) By the early 1700s there was effectively no trace of Ajuran left in Banaadir.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-:3-25)
Taxation and the practice of primae noctis were the main catalysts for the revolts against Ajuran rulers.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-80) The loss of port cities and fertile farms meant that much needed sources of revenue were lost to the rebels.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Lewis_1960_213%E2%80%93230-79) Somali maritime enterprise significantly declined after the collapse of the Ajuran Empire. However, other principalities such as the Isaaq Sultanate, Warsangali Sultanate, Majeerteen Sultanate, and the Sultanate of Hobyo in a way ensured its continuity.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-81)

From the alliance perspective, the Ajuran state was not an integral territorial one but one composed of a series of clan territories held together by the agnatic and affinal ties of their occupants. Wherever a Hawiyya group had settled and could be incorporated into the Garen alliance system, the "state" could be said to exist. On the local level, the system of rewards and spoils functioned in the traditional manner of the segmentary lineage system. The only difference was that the techniques of Ajuran administration and economic organization, and the prestige of the Imamate -- the imported technology and ideology, so to speak -- were extended to the newly incorporated areas, and a portion of the wealth flowed periodically to the center. If we hold to the hypothesis that Garen supremacy in Ajuran times rested largely on their centrality in the Hawiyya alliance system, we must see if the decline of Ajuran power is explicable by means of the alliance model. The fact is that the demise and supposed "disappearance" of the Ajuran is closely linked in tradition with the eclipse of the line of Jambelle Hawiyya and the political ascendancy of the Gurgate. Sometime between 1600 and 1625, the last Mudaffar governor of Mogadishu died at the hands of the militant nomads who lived on the outskirts of the town (25). Tradition remembers these nomads as the Hirab or Darandolle, which would make them descendants of Gurgate Hawiyya. For some time they had been migrating southward in what appears to have been a second phase of Hawiyya
(25) Cerulli, Somalia II, 245-51; Rovatti, "Mogadiscio," ASMAI pos. 87/1, f. 7.
P37

movement toward the Benaadir. Their ambush of the Mudaffar governor marked the end of Ajuran dominance of Mogadishu and the start of Darandolle penetration of the town's economic and political life. These same Darandolle then challenged Ajuran authority directly. They refused to comply with the Imam's edict which prohibited them from watering their herds at a particular set of wells during the daylight hours. In rebelling, the Darandolle rallied around an Imam of their own, who tradition says was born with a ring on his finger, a sign of his future preeminence (26). The clan into which this "rival" Imam was born was the Abgal, the very descendants of the aforementioned union between Faduma Sirjele (Garen) and Osman Darandolle. The implication is clear: The Darandolle Gurgate were advancing their claim to the title previously held in the line of Jambelle. The claim was made not merely on the basis of superior numbers, which the Gurgate always seem to have had, but also on the grounds that they too now possessed the superior baraka of the line of Balad, baraka acquired through their successive marriages into his family. One Abgal tradition in fact records a prophecy made to Sirjele Garen following his daughter's marriage to Osman Darandolle (27). Its thrust was that the sons of the new union (namely, the line of Abgal) would come to outnumber
(26) The fullest account of this tradition is "L'Anello dell'Imam: Leggenda de Uergadi," Somalia d'Oggi 1/1 (1956), 24-25.
(27) Cerulli, Somalia II, 243-4. the sons of Ajuran and drive them from the land.

By 1700, the new Imam had taken up residence in the Shangani quarter of Mogadishu, where he remained not only Imam of the Abgal, but titular head of the town as well. This was not the only instance of Gurgate success. Toward the close of the 17th century, the Sil'is Gurgate (see chart) appear in Benaadir traditions as masters of the region between Afgoy and Dafet. The character of their rule is strongly reminiscent of the Ajuran. The Sil'is sultan enjoyed the ius primae noctis. He exacted tribute from the surrounding populations -- by then largely Rahanweyn Somali -- in the form of durra and bun (a delicacy of coffee beans roasted in animal fat). Taxes were imposed on all stock that came to water at the river. The people were compelled to pray at the mosque in Lama Jiidle, the center of Sil'is administration. Finally, the Sil'is apparently formed an alliance with one section of the surrounding Rahanweyn population, who placed saab (conical wicker casings) on the roof peaks of their houses to signify their immunity from Sil'is retribution in times of war (28). Some of my Geledi (Rahanweyn) informants said that the Sil'is were actually that section of the Ajuran who governed the Afgoy district. While revealing an unawareness of the historical rivalry within the Hawiyya lineage system, the informants' statements attest to the continuity and similarity of Ajuran and Sil'is rule.
(28) Interviews with Ali Omar "Haji Goyle," Mogadishu, 10 June 1971; and Yusuf Nur, Mogadishu, 17 June 1971.

Finally, in the vicinity of Merka, a mysterious group known as the El-Amir made their appearance, again in the years between 1650 and 1700. According to a tradition collected by Guillain in 1847, a leader called “Amir” formed a “tribe” which invaded the territory of Merka and dispelled the Ajuran. They ruled for 34 years until the Bimal (Dir clan family) definitively occupied Merka (29). It is tempting to view this Amir as a warrior - administrator who seceded from the Ajuran state and formed a petty state of his own. Bimal traditions (30), which appear to associate the end of Ajuran rule with their defeat of an emir, lend support to such a view. Guillain suggested that the El - Amir were Abgal; if they were, their assumption of power would follow a pattern of Gurgate supremacy following an Ajuran decline (31). The picture which emerges is of a chain reaction of rebellions against Garen - Ajuran authority, resulting in the formation of a few localized successor states with leadership vested in Gurgate clans. These new polities maintained for a time the form and much of the substance of Ajuran rule, which accounts for their indistinguishability from the original Ajuran in many (particularly non - Hawiyya) traditions.
(29) Guillain, Documents III, 141-2, 147 n. 1. If Guillain's figures are accurate, the Bimal took Merka in 1690.
(30) See Gherardo Pantano, Nel Benadir: La Citta di Merca e La Regione Bimal (Livorno, 1910), 41 ff.; Barile, La colonizzazione fascista, 66 ff.

### Learning Objective
*   Explain the impact the arrival of Islam had on Somalia

### Key Points
*   During the Middle Ages, Somalia’s territory witnessed the emergence and decline of several powerful sultanates that dominated the regional trade. At no point was the region centralized as one state, and the development of all the sultanates was linked to the central role that Islam played in the area since the 7th century.  
*   The Sultanate of Mogadishu was an important trading empire that lasted from the 10th century to the 16th century. It maintained a vast trading network, dominated the regional gold trade, minted its own Mogadishu currency, and left an extensive architectural legacy in present-day southern Somalia.  
*   The Ajuran Sultanate ruled over large parts of the Horn of Africa between the 13th and late 17th centuries. Through a strong centralized administration and an aggressive military stance towards invaders, it successfully resisted an Oromo invasion from the west and a Portuguese incursion from the east. It left an extensive architectural and engineering legacy.  
*   The Warsangali Sultanate was a kingdom centered in northeastern and in some parts of southeastern Somalia. It was one of the largest sultanates ever established in the territory.  
*   The Sultanate of Ifat was a medieval Muslim Sultanate in the Horn of Africa.Led by the Walashma dynasty, it was centered in the ancient cities of Zeila and Shewa. The Kingdom ruled over parts of what are now eastern Ethiopia, Djibouti, and northern Somalia. Ifat first emerged in the 13th century, when Sultan Umar Walashma conquered the Sultanate of Showa in 1285. The Adal Sultanate or Kingdom of Adal was founded after the fall of the Sultanate of Ifat.It flourished from around 1415 to 1577.  
*   Following the Middle Ages and Early Modern period, Arab sultanates continued to dominate the region until it fell under the colonial control of Europeans in the 19th century.

### Terms
#### Berbers
An ethnic group indigenous to North Africa. They are distributed in an area stretching from the Atlantic Ocean to the Siwa Oasis in Egypt, and from the Mediterranean Sea to the Niger River. Since the Muslim conquest of North Africa in the 7th century, a large number inhabiting the Maghreb have acquired different degrees of knowledge of the various languages of North Africa.

### Terms
#### Zeila
A port city in northwestern Somali. It evolved into an early Islamic center with the arrival of Muslims shortly after the hijra. By the 9th century it was the capital of the Ifat Sultanate and a major port for its successor state the Adal Sultanate. It would attain its height of prosperity a few centuries later, in the 16th century. The city subsequently came under Ottoman and British protection in the 18th century.

### Terms
#### hijra
The migration or journey of the Islamic prophet Muhammad and his followers from Mecca to Yathrib, later renamed Medina, in 622 CE. In May 622 CE, after being warned of a plot to assassinate him, Muhammad secretly left his home in Mecca to emigrate to Yathrib, 320 kilometers (200 miles) north of Mecca, along with his companion, Abu Bakr.

## Somali Sultanates and Islam
During the Middle Ages, Somalia’s territory witnessed the emergence and decline of several powerful sultanates that dominated the regional trade. At no point was the region centralized as one state, and the development of all the sultanates was linked to the central role that Islam played in the area since the 7th century. Islam was introduced to the northern Somali coast from the Arabian Peninsula early on, shortly after the hijra (also hegira), or the journey of the Islamic prophet Muhammad and his followers from Mecca to Yathrib, later renamed Medina, in 622 CE.
The oldest mosque in the city of Zeila, a major port/trading center, dates to the 7th century.In the late 9th century, Muslims were living along the northern Somali seaboard, and evidence suggests that Zeila was already the headquarters of a Muslim sultanate in the 9th or 10th century. According to I.M. Lewis, the polity was governed by local dynasties consisting of Somalized Arabs or Arabized Somalis, who also ruled over the Sultanate of Mogadishu in the Benadir region to the south.

## Mogadishu
The Sultanate of Mogadishu was an important trading empire that lasted from the 10th century to the 16th century. It rose as one of the pre-eminent powers in the Horn of Africa over the course of the 12th to 14th centuries, before becoming part of the expanding Ajuran Empire. The Mogadishu Sultanate maintained a vast trading network, dominated the regional gold trade, minted its own Mogadishu currency, and left an extensive architectural legacy in present-day southern Somalia. Its first dynasty was established by Sultan Fakr ad-Din. This ruling house was succeeded by the Muzaffar dynasty, and the kingdom subsequently became closely linked with the Ajuran Sultanate.For many years, Mogadishu stood as the pre-eminent city in what is known as the Land of the Berbers, which was the medieval Arab term for the Somali coast. Contemporary historians suggest that the Berbers were ancestors of the modern Somalis.
Location of Mogadishu Sultanate according to 15th-century Italian cartographer Fra Mauro. During his travels, Ibn Sa’id al-Maghribi(1213–1286) noted that the city had already become the leading Islamic center in the region. By the time of the Moroccan traveler Ibn Battuta’s appearance on the Somali coast in 1331, the city was at the zenith of its prosperity. He described Mogadishu as “an exceedingly large city” with many rich merchants that was famous for its high quality fabric that it exported to Egypt, among other places.

## Ajuran
The Ajuran Sultanate ruled over large parts of the Horn of Africa between the 13th and late 17th centuries. Through a strong centralized administration and an aggressive military stance toward invaders, it successfully resisted an Oromo invasion (a series of expansions in the 16th and 17th centuries by the Oromo people from parts of Kenya and Somalia to Ethiopia)from the west and a Portuguese incursion from the east during the Gaal Madow and the Ajuran-Portuguese wars. Trading routes dating from the ancient and early medieval periods of Somali maritime enterprise were strengthened or re-established, and foreign trade and commerce in the coastal provinces flourished, with ships sailing to and coming from many kingdoms and empires in East Asia, South Asia, Europe, the Near East, North Africa, and East Africa.
The Ajuran Sultanate left an extensive architectural legacy, being one of the major medieval Somali powers engaged in castle and fortress building. Many of the ruined fortifications dotting the landscapes of southern Somalia today are attributed to the Ajuran Sultanate’s engineers. During the Ajuran period, many regions and people in the southern part of the Horn of Africa converted to Islam because of the theocratic nature of the government. The royal family, the House of Garen, expanded its territories and established its hegemonic rule through a skillful combination of warfare, trade linkages, and alliances.
As a hydraulic empire, the Ajuran monopolized the water resources of the Shebelle and Jubba rivers. It also constructed many of the limestone wells and cisterns of the state that are still in use today. The rulers developed new systems for agriculture and taxation, which continued to be used in parts of the Horn of Africa as late as the 19th century. The tyrannical rule of the later Ajuran rulers caused multiple rebellions to break out in the sultanate, and at the end of the 17th century the Ajuran state disintegrated into several successor kingdoms and states, the most prominent being the Geledi Sultanate.

## Warsangali
The Warsangali Sultanate was a kingdom centered in northeastern and in some parts of southeastern Somalia. It was one of the largest sultanates ever established in the territory, and, at the height of its power, included the Sanaag region and parts of the northeastern Bari region of the country, an area historically known as Maakhir or the Maakhir Coast. The Sultanate was founded in the late 13th century in northern Somalia by a group of Somalis from the Warsangali branch of the Darod clan. It survived until the British colonization of the region in the 19th century.
The Ajuuraan, Adal, and Warsangali Sultanates in the 15th century.Already in the classical (ancient) period, the Somali city-states of Mosylon, Opone, Malao, Sarapion, Mundus, Essina, and Tabae developed a lucrative trade network connecting with merchants from Phoenicia, Ptolemic Egypt, Greece, Parthian Persia, Sheba, Nabataea, and the Roman Empire. They used the ancient Somali maritime vessel known as the beden to transport their cargo.

It survived until the British colonization of the region in the 19th century.
The Ajuuraan, Adal, and Warsangali Sultanates in the 15th century.Already in the classical (ancient) period, the Somali city-states of Mosylon, Opone, Malao, Sarapion, Mundus, Essina, and Tabae developed a lucrative trade network connecting with merchants from Phoenicia, Ptolemic Egypt, Greece, Parthian Persia, Sheba, Nabataea, and the Roman Empire. They used the ancient Somali maritime vessel known as the beden to transport their cargo.

texts.9:
### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
Over the next decades tensions remained high and the increased contact between Somali sailors and Ottomancorsairs worried the Portuguese who sent a punitive expedition under João de Sepúlveda, where he bombarded Mogadishu and captured Turkish vessels, compelling its ruler to sign a peace deal with the Portuguese. Barawa would also sign peace with the Portuguese after being sacked.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-52)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Sep%C3%BAlveda,_1542-53) The Ottoman-Somali cooperation against the Portuguese on the Indian Ocean reached a high point in the 1580s when Ajuran clients of the coastal cities began to cooperate with the Arabs and Swahilis under Portuguese rule and sent an envoy to the Turkish corsair Mir Ali Bey for a joint expedition against the Portuguese. He agreed and was joined by a Somali fleet in order to attack the Portuguese colonies in Southeast Africa.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch195025-54)
A 16th century map by Jan Huyghen[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-55)
texts.10:
### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
The Somali-Ottoman offensive managed to drive out the Portuguese from several important cities such as Pate, Mombasa and Kilwa. However, the Portuguese governor sent envoys to Portuguese India requesting a large Portuguese fleet. This request was answered and it reversed the previous offensive of the Muslims into one of defense. The Portuguese armada managed to re-take most of the lost cities and began punishing their leaders, but they refrained from attacking Mogadishu, securing the city's autonomy in the Indian Ocean.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Cites-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-57) The Ottoman Empire would remain an economic partner.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Shapes-12) Throughout the 16th and 17th centuries the Ajurans successively defied Portuguese hegemony on the Indian Ocean by employing a new coinage which followed the Ottoman pattern, thus proclaiming an attitude of economic independence in regard to the Portuguese.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-61)

### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
From the late 15th and up until the 17th centuries saw the arrival of Muslim families from Arabia, Persia, India and Spain to the Ajuran realm of territories, the majority of whom settled in the coastal provinces. Some migrated because of the instability in their respective regions, as was the case with the Hadhrami families from Yemen and Muslims from Spain fleeing the Inquisition.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-62)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-63) Others came to conduct business or for religious purposes. Due to their strong tradition in religious learning, the new Muslim communities also enjoyed high status among the Somali ruling elite and commoners.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-65)
The tomb of Sheikh Hussein
The most famous Somali scholar of Islam from the Ajuraan period is Sheikh Hussein, who was born in Merca, one of the power jurisdiction and cultural centers of the Ajuran Empire.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-66) He is credited with converting the Sidamo people living in the area of what is now the Bale Province, Ethiopia to Islam.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-67) He is also credited with establishing the Sultanate of Bale.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-69)
Despite the Bale Sultanate not being directly under Ajuran rule, the two kingdoms were deeply connected and Bale was heavily influenced by Ajuran. His tomb lies in the town of Sheikh Hussein in what is considered the most sacred place in the country for Ethiopian Muslims, in particular those of Oromo ethnic descent.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-71)

### Fall of Benadir and Southern Somalia
[edit]
The Ajuran Empire slowly declined in power at the end of the 17th century. In this period the rulers of the empire abandoned Sharia, became oppressive and enacted heavy taxation.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-:4-9) The dethronement of the Muzaffar clients in Mogadishu and other coastal cities by the Abgaalimam who then established the Hiraab Imamate taking residence in Mogadishu was a significant setback,[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTELewis198837-77) and the defeat of the Silcis vassals by a former Ajuran general in the interior of the state, Ibrahim Adeer, who established the Gobroon dynasty.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-78)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Lewis_1960_213%E2%80%93230-79) By the early 1700s there was effectively no trace of Ajuran left in Banaadir.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-:3-25)
Taxation and the practice of primae noctis were the main catalysts for the revolts against Ajuran rulers.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-80) The loss of port cities and fertile farms meant that much needed sources of revenue were lost to the rebels.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Lewis_1960_213%E2%80%93230-79) Somali maritime enterprise significantly declined after the collapse of the Ajuran Empire. However, other principalities such as the Isaaq Sultanate, Warsangali Sultanate, Majeerteen Sultanate, and the Sultanate of Hobyo in a way ensured its continuity.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-81)

From the alliance perspective, the Ajuran state was not an integral territorial one but one composed of a series of clan territories held together by the agnatic and affinal ties of their occupants. Wherever a Hawiyya group had settled and could be incorporated into the Garen alliance system, the "state" could be said to exist. On the local level, the system of rewards and spoils functioned in the traditional manner of the segmentary lineage system. The only difference was that the techniques of Ajuran administration and economic organization, and the prestige of the Imamate -- the imported technology and ideology, so to speak -- were extended to the newly incorporated areas, and a portion of the wealth flowed periodically to the center. If we hold to the hypothesis that Garen supremacy in Ajuran times rested largely on their centrality in the Hawiyya alliance system, we must see if the decline of Ajuran power is explicable by means of the alliance model. The fact is that the demise and supposed "disappearance" of the Ajuran is closely linked in tradition with the eclipse of the line of Jambelle Hawiyya and the political ascendancy of the Gurgate. Sometime between 1600 and 1625, the last Mudaffar governor of Mogadishu died at the hands of the militant nomads who lived on the outskirts of the town (25). Tradition remembers these nomads as the Hirab or Darandolle, which would make them descendants of Gurgate Hawiyya. For some time they had been migrating southward in what appears to have been a second phase of Hawiyya
(25) Cerulli, Somalia II, 245-51; Rovatti, "Mogadiscio," ASMAI pos. 87/1, f. 7.

texts.17:
movement toward the Benaadir. Their ambush of the Mudaffar governor marked the end of Ajuran dominance of Mogadishu and the start of Darandolle penetration of the town's economic and political life. These same Darandolle then challenged Ajuran authority directly. They refused to comply with the Imam's edict which prohibited them from watering their herds at a particular set of wells during the daylight hours. In rebelling, the Darandolle rallied around an Imam of their own, who tradition says was born with a ring on his finger, a sign of his future preeminence (26). The clan into which this "rival" Imam was born was the Abgal, the very descendants of the aforementioned union between Faduma Sirjele (Garen) and Osman Darandolle. The implication is clear: The Darandolle Gurgate were advancing their claim to the title previously held in the line of Jambelle. The claim was made not merely on the basis of superior numbers, which the Gurgate always seem to have had, but also on the grounds that they too now possessed the superior baraka of the line of Balad, baraka acquired through their successive marriages into his family. One Abgal tradition in fact records a prophecy made to Sirjele Garen following his daughter's marriage to Osman Darandolle (27). Its thrust was that the sons of the new union (namely, the line of Abgal) would come to outnumber

By 1700, the new Imam had taken up residence in the Shangani quarter of Mogadishu, where he remained not only Imam of the Abgal, but titular head of the town as well. This was not the only instance of Gurgate success. Toward the close of the 17th century, the Sil'is Gurgate (see chart) appear in Benaadir traditions as masters of the region between Afgoy and Dafet. The character of their rule is strongly reminiscent of the Ajuran. The Sil'is sultan enjoyed the ius primae noctis. He exacted tribute from the surrounding populations -- by then largely Rahanweyn Somali -- in the form of durra and bun (a delicacy of coffee beans roasted in animal fat). Taxes were imposed on all stock that came to water at the river. The people were compelled to pray at the mosque in Lama Jiidle, the center of Sil'is administration. Finally, the Sil'is apparently formed an alliance with one section of the surrounding Rahanweyn population, who placed saab (conical wicker casings) on the roof peaks of their houses to signify their immunity from Sil'is retribution in times of war (28). Some of my Geledi (Rahanweyn) informants said that the Sil'is were actually that section of the Ajuran who governed the Afgoy district. While revealing an unawareness of the historical rivalry within the Hawiyya lineage system, the informants' statements attest to the continuity and similarity of Ajuran and Sil'is rule.

Finally, in the vicinity of Merka, a mysterious group known as the El-Amir made their appearance, again in the years between 1650 and 1700. According to a tradition collected by Guillain in 1847, a leader called “Amir” formed a “tribe” which invaded the territory of Merka and dispelled the Ajuran. They ruled for 34 years until the Bimal (Dir clan family) definitively occupied Merka (29). It is tempting to view this Amir as a warrior - administrator who seceded from the Ajuran state and formed a petty state of his own. Bimal traditions (30), which appear to associate the end of Ajuran rule with their defeat of an emir, lend support to such a view. Guillain suggested that the El - Amir were Abgal; if they were, their assumption of power would follow a pattern of Gurgate supremacy following an Ajuran decline (31). The picture which emerges is of a chain reaction of rebellions against Garen - Ajuran authority, resulting in the formation of a few localized successor states with leadership vested in Gurgate clans. These new polities maintained for a time the form and much of the substance of Ajuran rule, which accounts for their indistinguishability from the original Ajuran in many (particularly non - Hawiyya) traditions.
(29) Guillain, Documents III, 141-2, 147 n. 1. If Guillain's figures are accurate, the Bimal took Merka in 1690.
(30) See Gherardo Pantano, Nel Benadir: La Citta di Merca e La Regione Bimal (Livorno, 1910), 41 ff.; Barile, La colonizzazione fascista, 66 ff.
(31) It is also possible that Guillain wrote "El - Amir" for El - Hamar (people of Hamar, the Somali name for Mogadishu). Since the people of Hamar were by 1690 largely Abgal, the rendering of El - Hamar would not be contradictory.

### Learning Objective
*   Explain the impact the arrival of Islam had on Somalia

### Key Points
*   During the Middle Ages, Somalia’s territory witnessed the emergence and decline of several powerful sultanates that dominated the regional trade. At no point was the region centralized as one state, and the development of all the sultanates was linked to the central role that Islam played in the area since the 7th century.  
*   The Sultanate of Mogadishu was an important trading empire that lasted from the 10th century to the 16th century. It maintained a vast trading network, dominated the regional gold trade, minted its own Mogadishu currency, and left an extensive architectural legacy in present-day southern Somalia.  
*   The Ajuran Sultanate ruled over large parts of the Horn of Africa between the 13th and late 17th centuries. Through a strong centralized administration and an aggressive military stance towards invaders, it successfully resisted an Oromo invasion from the west and a Portuguese incursion from the east. It left an extensive architectural and engineering legacy.  
*   The Warsangali Sultanate was a kingdom centered in northeastern and in some parts of southeastern Somalia. It was one of the largest sultanates ever established in the territory.  
*   The Sultanate of Ifat was a medieval Muslim Sultanate in the Horn of Africa.Led by the Walashma dynasty, it was centered in the ancient cities of Zeila and Shewa. The Kingdom ruled over parts of what are now eastern Ethiopia, Djibouti, and northern Somalia. Ifat first emerged in the 13th century, when Sultan Umar Walashma conquered the Sultanate of Showa in 1285. The Adal Sultanate or Kingdom of Adal was founded after the fall of the Sultanate of Ifat.It flourished from around 1415 to 1577.  
*   Following the Middle Ages and Early Modern period, Arab sultanates continued to dominate the region until it fell under the colonial control of Europeans in the 19th century.

### Terms
#### Berbers
An ethnic group indigenous to North Africa. They are distributed in an area stretching from the Atlantic Ocean to the Siwa Oasis in Egypt, and from the Mediterranean Sea to the Niger River. Since the Muslim conquest of North Africa in the 7th century, a large number inhabiting the Maghreb have acquired different degrees of knowledge of the various languages of North Africa.

### Terms
#### Zeila
A port city in northwestern Somali. It evolved into an early Islamic center with the arrival of Muslims shortly after the hijra. By the 9th century it was the capital of the Ifat Sultanate and a major port for its successor state the Adal Sultanate. It would attain its height of prosperity a few centuries later, in the 16th century. The city subsequently came under Ottoman and British protection in the 18th century.

### Terms
#### hijra
The migration or journey of the Islamic prophet Muhammad and his followers from Mecca to Yathrib, later renamed Medina, in 622 CE. In May 622 CE, after being warned of a plot to assassinate him, Muhammad secretly left his home in Mecca to emigrate to Yathrib, 320 kilometers (200 miles) north of Mecca, along with his companion, Abu Bakr.

## Somali Sultanates and Islam
During the Middle Ages, Somalia’s territory witnessed the emergence and decline of several powerful sultanates that dominated the regional trade. At no point was the region centralized as one state, and the development of all the sultanates was linked to the central role that Islam played in the area since the 7th century. Islam was introduced to the northern Somali coast from the Arabian Peninsula early on, shortly after the hijra (also hegira), or the journey of the Islamic prophet Muhammad and his followers from Mecca to Yathrib, later renamed Medina, in 622 CE.
The oldest mosque in the city of Zeila, a major port/trading center, dates to the 7th century.In the late 9th century, Muslims were living along the northern Somali seaboard, and evidence suggests that Zeila was already the headquarters of a Muslim sultanate in the 9th or 10th century. According to I.M. Lewis, the polity was governed by local dynasties consisting of Somalized Arabs or Arabized Somalis, who also ruled over the Sultanate of Mogadishu in the Benadir region to the south.

## Mogadishu
The Sultanate of Mogadishu was an important trading empire that lasted from the 10th century to the 16th century. It rose as one of the pre-eminent powers in the Horn of Africa over the course of the 12th to 14th centuries, before becoming part of the expanding Ajuran Empire. The Mogadishu Sultanate maintained a vast trading network, dominated the regional gold trade, minted its own Mogadishu currency, and left an extensive architectural legacy in present-day southern Somalia. Its first dynasty was established by Sultan Fakr ad-Din. This ruling house was succeeded by the Muzaffar dynasty, and the kingdom subsequently became closely linked with the Ajuran Sultanate.For many years, Mogadishu stood as the pre-eminent city in what is known as the Land of the Berbers, which was the medieval Arab term for the Somali coast. Contemporary historians suggest that the Berbers were ancestors of the modern Somalis.
Location of Mogadishu Sultanate according to 15th-century Italian cartographer Fra Mauro. During his travels, Ibn Sa’id al-Maghribi(1213–1286) noted that the city had already become the leading Islamic center in the region. By the time of the Moroccan traveler Ibn Battuta’s appearance on the Somali coast in 1331, the city was at the zenith of its prosperity. He described Mogadishu as “an exceedingly large city” with many rich merchants that was famous for its high quality fabric that it exported to Egypt, among other places.

## Ajuran
The Ajuran Sultanate ruled over large parts of the Horn of Africa between the 13th and late 17th centuries. Through a strong centralized administration and an aggressive military stance toward invaders, it successfully resisted an Oromo invasion (a series of expansions in the 16th and 17th centuries by the Oromo people from parts of Kenya and Somalia to Ethiopia)from the west and a Portuguese incursion from the east during the Gaal Madow and the Ajuran-Portuguese wars. Trading routes dating from the ancient and early medieval periods of Somali maritime enterprise were strengthened or re-established, and foreign trade and commerce in the coastal provinces flourished, with ships sailing to and coming from many kingdoms and empires in East Asia, South Asia, Europe, the Near East, North Africa, and East Africa.
The Ajuran Sultanate left an extensive architectural legacy, being one of the major medieval Somali powers engaged in castle and fortress building. Many of the ruined fortifications dotting the landscapes of southern Somalia today are attributed to the Ajuran Sultanate’s engineers. During the Ajuran period, many regions and people in the southern part of the Horn of Africa converted to Islam because of the theocratic nature of the government. The royal family, the House of Garen, expanded its territories and established its hegemonic rule through a skillful combination of warfare, trade linkages, and alliances.
As a hydraulic empire, the Ajuran monopolized the water resources of the Shebelle and Jubba rivers. It also constructed many of the limestone wells and cisterns of the state that are still in use today. The rulers developed new systems for agriculture and taxation, which continued to be used in parts of the Horn of Africa as late as the 19th century. The tyrannical rule of the later Ajuran rulers caused multiple rebellions to break out in the sultanate, and at the end of the 17th century the Ajuran state disintegrated into several successor kingdoms and states, the most prominent being the Geledi Sultanate.

## Warsangali
The Warsangali Sultanate was a kingdom centered in northeastern and in some parts of southeastern Somalia. It was one of the largest sultanates ever established in the territory, and, at the height of its power, included the Sanaag region and parts of the northeastern Bari region of the country, an area historically known as Maakhir or the Maakhir Coast. The Sultanate was founded in the late 13th century in northern Somalia by a group of Somalis from the Warsangali branch of the Darod clan. It survived until the British colonization of the region in the 19th century.

**Short answer**

When the Ajuran Sultanate (the medieval Somali‑Muslim state that ruled the Horn of Africa from the 13th to the 17th century) decided to write its own coinage, it was signalling the end of foreign domination—namely the Portuguese— and the re‑assertion of its own sovereignty.  
The “people from whom the new coins were a proclamation of independence” were the Portuguese (and, more broadly, the European trading powers who had established footholds along the Somali coast). They were expelled from the Ajuran realm through a mixture of naval battles, sieges of key port‑cities, diplomatic agreements, and the enforcement of a local tax‑and‑tribute system. The minting of native Ajuran coins further formalised the Emperor’s newfound autonomy.

**In detail**

| Stage | What happened | How it was done | Result |
|-------|---------------|-----------------|--------|
| **Early Portuguese incursion** |  Portuguese traders began to establish outposts along the Somali coast (Mombasa, Pate, Kilwa, and later Mogadishu). | Their presence was tolerated only by mutual trade; the Ajuran Sultanate recognised them as a threat to its monopoly on the Indian‑Ocean trade network. | The Sultanate began to seek alliances (with the Ottoman Empire) and defined a “Portuguese frontier” in its diplomatic correspondence. |
| **Clash at Mogadishu (1543‑1544)** | A Portuguese punitive expedition led by João de Sepúlveda bombarded Mogadishu and captured Turkish merchant vessels. | The Ajuran governor was forced into a temporary peace with the Portuguese to avoid complete destruction of his capital. | The incident exposed the weakness of Portuguese trade posts; the Ajuran used it to rally a coastal coalition. |
| **Coalition with the Ottomans / ``Sultan’s Decree’’** | The Ajuran delegation (including the Admiral Mir Ali Bey) brought Turkish war‑ships to aid against the Portuguese. | A joint expedition laid pressure on Portuguese garrisons; the Ajuran imposed a decree confiscating Portuguese property and travellers, forcing a withdrawal. | Portuguese influence in Mogadishu and neighbouring coasts was forced back to a temporary cease‑fire. |
| **Siege of Mombasa, Pate & Kilwa (late‑16th century)** | The Ajuran fleet, supported by Ottoman gun‑boats, blockaded French‑Portuguese posts and sacked Portuguese supply depots. | The sustained naval blockade, raiding of Portuguese trade goods and local support for the Afar/Oromo tribes made Portuguese garrisons untenable. | Portuguese withdrawal from the key ports; the “Ajuran‑controlled” channel remained open to Muslim traders. |
| **Re‑assertion of sovereignty (c. 1560‑1580)** | After the defeats, the Ajuran Sultanate re‑established its dominion over the hinterland and the Somali coast. | A new tax‑and‑tribute system was re‑implemented (linked to the irrigation “aqueduct” system the Ajuran had engineered). | Control over the coastal trade and the interior’s irrigation flowed back into the Ajuran state. |
| **Minting new Ajuran coins** | The Ajuran sultans (notably Imad Al‑Bâla’a?) started producing bronze coins bearing the Sultan’s name and the Arabic word **“Sultanate”**. | The new coins used an Ottoman‑style design, signalling that the Ajuran had adopted an independent monetary system. | The coins served as a tangible, daily reminder of Ajuran sovereignty; they were minted and circulated widely, especially in the Benadir (bahr‑district) cities. |

**Result**

The expulsion of Portuguese traders and the minting of native Ajuran coins were linked events. By force of arms and diplomacy, the Ajuran expelled Europeans from its territory. The decisive moment came when the Ajuran re‑established control over Mogadishu and the key Indian‑Ocean ports in the 1560s, ending Portuguese colonial occupation, and the subsequent coinage became a public symbol of that reclaimed independence. The “people” involved were the Portuguese—foreign merchants and garrisons—whose expulsion enabled the Ajuran Sultanate to issue its own, sovereign currency.
